sections.heading: WHY THIS PASSAGE
sections.body:
Pride and brotherhood are directly connected — you can’t fully have one without dealing with the other. Pride is almost always the thing that keeps a guy from actually being known, asking for help, receiving correction, or admitting he’s struggling. Real brotherhood requires humility on both ends: the humility to be honest about your own life, and the humility to speak truth to someone else without superiority.

This week brings both together. Philippians 2 gives the ultimate model — Christ emptying Himself instead of holding onto status. Proverbs 16 warns what happens when pride goes unchecked. Ecclesiastes 4 makes the case for why you need other people at all. And 1 Peter 5 ties it together — humility toward each other is what actually makes brotherhood possible.

“The guys who are hardest to know are usually the guys with the most pride to protect. Humility is what opens the door to brotherhood.”

sections.heading: SCRIPTURE PASSAGES (ESV)
sections.body:
Philippians 2:3–8

3 Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves.

4 Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.

5 Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus,

6 who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,

7 but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.

8 And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

Proverbs 16:18

18 Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

Ecclesiastes 4:9–12

9 Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.

10 For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!

11 Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone?

12 And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him. A threefold cord is not quickly broken.

1 Peter 5:5–6

5 Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

6 Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you.

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE to open. These get guys thinking about both pride and connection right from the start.

  1. Is it harder for you to say ‘I’m sorry’ or ‘I need help’? Why do you think that is? — gets at two common faces of pride, sets up the brotherhood tie-in

  2. Who’s the most humble guy you know personally? Does he have close friends who really know him? Is that a coincidence? — directly links humility and real friendship before the passage even opens

  3. Has there ever been a time you didn’t ask for help because you didn’t want to look like you needed it? What happened? — vulnerable opener that sets up both themes

  4. Do you think you struggle with pride? Most guys say no right away — what makes you so sure? — a little provocative, good if the group is ready to be challenged early

Leader tip: This week connects two ideas, so it helps to name the link early: ‘Pride is usually what keeps guys from real brotherhood — that’s what we’re getting into today.’

sections.heading: 2 — CONTEXT (6–10 MIN)
sections.body:
After reading through the passages together, share this background before discussion:

Philippians 2:3–8 — The Ultimate Example of Humility

  • Paul writes this to a church dealing with internal rivalry and selfish ambition among its members — division caused by pride.

  • Before the theology, Paul gives the practical command: count others more significant than yourselves.

  • Then he points to Jesus as proof — God didn’t grasp at status, He emptied himself and became a servant.

  • If God didn’t need to protect His position, that’s the strongest possible argument that we don’t need to protect ours either.

Proverbs 16:18 — Pride Before a Fall

  • One of the most quoted proverbs — usually applied to other people, rarely to ourselves.

  • “Haughty spirit” describes an inflated self-view that can’t see its own blind spots.

  • The fall often comes specifically because pride refuses correction or warning — the kind correction a real friend would offer, if you’d let him.

Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 — Why You Need Other People

  • Even in a book known for its honesty about life’s hardships, companionship is named as genuinely good.

  • “If they fall, one will lift up his fellow” — but pride is exactly what keeps a guy from letting someone lift him up.

  • “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” — the strength of brotherhood depends on guys being willing to actually be in it together, not just near each other.

1 Peter 5:5–6 — Where Pride and Brotherhood Meet

  • Peter uses clothing language — humility isn’t natural, it’s something you intentionally put on, especially ‘toward one another.’

  • “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” — pride doesn’t just block friendship, it actually works against you spiritually.

  • This verse makes the connection explicit: humility toward each other is what makes real brotherhood possible at all.

“You can’t be fully known by someone you’re still performing for. Humility is what lets people actually in.”

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: WHERE PRIDE BLOCKS BROTHERHOOD (12 MIN)
sections.body:
These questions connect pride directly to the relationships in the room — not pride in the abstract, but the specific ways it shows up between guys who actually know each other. Pick what fits.

  1. Is there something going on in your life right now that nobody in this room knows about — and is pride part of why?

  2. When someone in this group has challenged you or given you feedback, what’s your honest first reaction, even if you don’t show it?

  3. Ecclesiastes says woe to the one who falls alone with no one to lift him up. Have you ever stayed silent about a struggle because you didn’t want to seem weak in front of other guys?

  4. Do you find it easy or hard to celebrate someone else’s win — especially someone in this room — if it’s in an area you care about too?

  5. Is there a guy in this group you’ve been unwilling to be fully honest with because part of you wants to look like you’ve got it together?

  6. What does your pride usually protect when you’re around other guys? What are you afraid would happen if you let your guard down here?

  7. Have you ever had a friend confront you and it actually helped? What made you receive it instead of getting defensive?

Leader tip: Question 1 and 6 are the heaviest here — and they’re also the most direct test of how far this group has actually come. Given how open the last few weeks have been, this group may be ready for it. Be ready to go first.

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: HUMILITY THAT BUILDS BROTHERHOOD (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Move from diagnosis to practice. These questions look at what it actually takes — on both ends — to let humility build real brotherhood instead of just talking about it.

  1. Jesus had every right to status and didn’t grasp for it. What’s something you feel like you need to prove to the guys in this room that you could just let go of?

  2. What would it look like to ‘count someone more significant’ than yourself with a specific guy in this group this week?

  3. Iron sharpens iron through friction, not just comfort. Is there someone here who needs to hear something honest from you, out of love? What’s stopping you?

  4. Would you actually want to be challenged by the guys in this room if you started drifting? What would you need from them to receive it well?

  5. 1 Peter says clothe yourselves with humility toward one another. What’s one specific way you could practice that with this group, not just in general?

  6. What would change in this group if every guy here actually believed God gives grace to the humble — and chose humility over always being right?

Leader tip: Question 4 connects directly back to brotherhood and gives guys a chance to say what they actually need from each other — useful information for how the group operates going forward, not just talk.

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Jesus had more reason for pride than anyone who has ever lived — and chose the opposite, becoming a servant instead of protecting His status. The brotherhood you’re building in this room only goes as deep as the humility each guy is willing to bring to it. Pride keeps you isolated even in a room full of people. Humility is what actually lets you be known.

“A threefold cord is not quickly broken — but it’s only strong if every strand is willing to bend.”

Leave the group with one of these to carry into the week:

  1. Tell one guy in this room something real that you’ve been keeping to yourself out of pride. Commit to actually doing it this week. — direct accountability tied to both themes

  2. Is there an apology you need to give — to someone here or elsewhere — that pride has been keeping you from? Commit to giving it.

  3. Pick one guy in this group and ask him to challenge you on something specific this week. Let him actually do it.

Close in prayer — pray specifically that pride wouldn’t keep anyone in the room isolated, and that the brotherhood here would keep deepening through real humility, not just good intentions.

Leader tip: This is a great week for the leader to model it directly — naming a specific way pride has kept you from being fully known by the group, even with how far you’ve all come. It gives permission for everyone else to do the same.

title: What Does This Man’s Life Say to Yours?

sections.heading: Intro
sections.body: Format: Read real letters from Paul, respond to the man behind them · ~60 min

sections.heading: HOW THIS SESSION WORKS
sections.body:
Tonight you’re not doing a topical study. You’re reading letters from a real man in hard situations and asking what his life says to yours. Paul wrote these words from prison, in exile, facing execution, and in the middle of conflict. He wasn’t writing theology for a textbook. He was writing to people he loved from a place of pressure.

Each letter gets read aloud together. Then you respond — not to a lesson, but to the man. What do you hear? What hits you? What do you want to push back on? The discussion questions are there if you need them, but follow the conversation first.

Leader tip: Read each passage slowly. These are letters — not bullet points. Let them land before anyone speaks. After each reading, start with one simple question: ‘What do you hear from this man?’ and see where it goes before pulling out the discussion questions.

sections.heading: LETTER 1 · PHILIPPIANS · 1:12–26
sections.body:
Context: Paul is in a Roman prison, chained to a guard, facing a possible death sentence. He has no idea if he’ll get out. He’s writing to a church he loves. This is what he says.

Philippians 1:12–26 (ESV)

12 I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel,

13 so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard and to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ.

14 And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment, are much more bold to speak the word of God without fear.

15 Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will.

16 The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel.

17 The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment.

18 What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,

19 for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my deliverance,

20 as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be ashamed in anything, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death.

21 For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

22 If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell.

23 I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better.

24 But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.

25 Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith,

26 so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again.

What to listen for

  • Paul is in chains and talking about joy. How does that work?

  • He says ‘to live is Christ and to die is gain’ — does he actually mean that, or is it a line?

  • He chooses to stay not for himself but for others. What does that kind of selflessness actually require?

sections.heading: DISCUSSION — LETTER 1
sections.body:
1. Paul is in prison writing about joy and advancement. What’s your honest reaction to that — inspired, skeptical, somewhere in between?

  2. He says ‘to live is Christ, to die is gain.’ Do you actually believe that — or does it sound like something you’re supposed to say?

  3. Paul’s suffering ended up advancing the gospel. Is there a hard season in your life right now that could be doing something you can’t fully see yet?

  4. He chose to stay alive for other people’s sake, not his own. What would it look like to make a decision in your life right now based entirely on what’s best for someone else?

  5. What does this man’s life say to yours right now? Just say what you hear.

sections.heading: LETTER 2 · 2 TIMOTHY · 4:6–18
sections.body:
Context: This is likely the last letter Paul ever wrote. He’s in a Roman dungeon, not a comfortable prison. He knows he’s about to be executed. He’s writing to Timothy — his closest son in the faith — for the last time.

2 Timothy 4:6–18 (ESV)

6 For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.

7 I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.

8 Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.

9 Do your best to come to me soon.

10 For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica.

11 Luke alone is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry.

16 At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. May it not be charged against them!

17 But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. So I was rescued from the lion’s mouth.

18 The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

What to listen for

  • His friends abandoned him. He’s alone. And he still says ‘the Lord stood by me.’

  • Demas left because he loved the world more than the mission. That’s a quiet, undramatic failure.

  • ‘I have kept the faith’ — that’s what he wants on his record at the end. Not his accomplishments. His faithfulness.

sections.heading: DISCUSSION — LETTER 2
sections.body:
1. This is a dying man’s last letter. What do you hear from him that you wouldn’t hear from someone who had more time?

  2. Paul says ‘I have kept the faith’ — not ‘I built something great’ or ‘I succeeded.’ What does it mean for that to be enough at the end of your life?

  3. Demas quietly walked away because he loved the world more. Is there a version of that happening slowly in your own life right now? What is the world offering you that’s competing with your faith?

  4. Everyone abandoned Paul at his trial. But he says ‘the Lord stood by me.’ Have you ever felt completely alone in something hard — and experienced that same reality? Or does it sound distant to you right now?

  5. If you wrote a letter like this at the end of your life, what would you want to be able to say honestly? What would you be afraid you couldn’t say?

sections.heading: LETTER 3 · PHILEMON · 1:8–19
sections.body:
Context: Paul is writing to Philemon — a wealthy Christian who owns a slave named Onesimus. Onesimus ran away, somehow ended up with Paul, became a believer, and now Paul is sending him back. Paul is asking Philemon to receive him not as a slave but as a brother. This is one of the most personal, uncomfortable letters in the entire Bible.

Philemon 1:8–19 (ESV)

8 Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required,

9 yet for love’s sake I prefer to appeal to you — I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus —

10 I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment.

11 (Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.)

12 I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart.

13 I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel,

14 but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.

15 For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever,

16 no longer as a bondservant but better than a bondservant, as a dear brother — especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

17 So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.

18 If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.

19 I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it — to say nothing of your owing me even your own self.

What to listen for

  • Paul doesn’t command — he appeals. He gives Philemon the choice. Why does that matter?

  • ‘Charge that to my account’ — Paul offers to absorb the cost of someone else’s failure. Sound familiar?

  • He’s asking Philemon to receive someone who wronged him as a brother. That’s radical forgiveness with a name and a face on it.

sections.heading: DISCUSSION — LETTER 3
sections.body:
1. Paul steps in between Philemon and someone who wronged him and says ‘put it on my tab.’ That’s a picture of what Jesus did for all of us. Does that land differently when you see it in a real human situation like this?

  2. Is there someone in your life who has wronged you that you’ve been holding at arm’s length? What would it look like to receive them the way Paul is asking Philemon to receive Onesimus?

  3. Paul appeals rather than commands — he gives Philemon the choice. Why does real love have to be chosen freely? What’s lost when you force it?

  4. Onesimus was ‘useless’ and became useful. Is there someone you’ve written off that God might not be finished with?

  5. What does this letter say to you personally — are you more like Paul, Philemon, or Onesimus in a situation in your life right now?

sections.heading: HOW TO CLOSE
sections.body:
After the three letters, bring it back to the man behind all of them. Paul wrote from prison, from loneliness, from the edge of death — and every letter is full of joy, purpose, and love for people. Close with this:

“Paul’s life didn’t look like success by any standard the world uses. But at the end he said ‘I have kept the faith.’ What do you want to be able to say at the end of yours?”

Let every guy answer. Don’t rush it. Then close in prayer — pray over what each man said he wants his life to mean.

Leader tip: If time is short, pick two of the three letters rather than rushing through all three. Letter 1 (joy in prison) and Letter 2 (last words) together make a complete session on their own.

sections.heading: Intro
sections.body: Format: Real-world scenarios debated through Scripture · ~60 min · 6 scenarios included, use 3–4

sections.heading: HOW THIS SESSION WORKS
sections.body:
Each scenario is a real-world situation with no easy answer. Read it out loud to the group, then let them debate what the right move is — before you bring in the Scripture. The goal isn’t to find a tidy answer. It’s to see how guys actually think through hard decisions and where the Bible’s wisdom lands.

You have 6 scenarios. Pick 3–4 based on what fits your group best and how the conversation flows. Some will go 5 minutes, some will go 20. Let the room decide.

Leader tip: The sequence matters. Start with a scenario that’s a little lighter — easier to debate, less personal. Save the heavier ones for when the room is warmed up. Suggested order: 1, 3, 5, then 2, 4, or 6 depending on where the group is.

sections.heading: FORMAT FOR EACH SCENARIO
sections.body:
1. Read the scenario out loud — don't editorialize, just read it.

  2. Ask: 'What do you do?' Let guys debate freely for a few minutes.

  3. Ask the follow-up questions to push deeper.

  4. Drop in the anchor verse and ask: 'Does this change anything?'

  5. Land it: 'So what’s the actual right move — and why is that hard?'

sections.heading: SCENARIO 1 · WORKPLACE · THE SHORTCUT
sections.body: You’ve been working hard for two years and you’re finally up for a promotion. Your manager pulls you aside and tells you the job is basically yours — but asks you to sign off on a report you know has some numbers that aren’t quite right. Nothing illegal, just… optimistic. Everyone does it. If you say no, someone else will sign it and probably get the promotion instead. What do you do?

sections.heading: Discussion questions:
sections.body:
1. Is this actually a big deal — or is it just how business works? Where’s the line?

  2. If you sign it and get the promotion, have you compromised something that can’t be undone? Or is it a one-time thing you move past?

  3. What do you tell yourself to justify it — and have you told yourself something like that before?

  4. Is the version of you that signs that report the man you’ve been trying to build in this group?

Proverbs 10:9 “Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out.”

Colossians 3:23 “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.”

sections.heading: SCENARIO 2 · LOYALTY & FRIENDSHIP · WHAT YOU KNOW
sections.body: One of your closest friends is engaged. You find out — not from him — that he’s been talking to his ex behind his fiancée’s back. Nothing physical, but it’s clearly more than it should be. He doesn’t know you know. His wedding is in three months. What do you do?

sections.heading: Discussion questions:
sections.body:
1. Do you say something — and if so, to him or to her? Or do you stay out of it entirely?

  2. What’s the most loving thing you can do here — for him, for her, for the relationship?

  3. Is staying silent the same as enabling it? Where’s the line between loyalty and covering for someone?

  4. If the situation were reversed — if you were the one doing this — what would you want your closest friend to do?

  5. Does your answer change if he’s a believer versus if he’s not?

Galatians 6:1 “Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness.”

Proverbs 27:6 “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.”

sections.heading: SCENARIO 3 · MONEY · THE WINDFALL
sections.body: You’re tight on money. You’ve been stressed about it for months. Out of nowhere, a billing error goes in your favor — a company charges you way less than they should have, and they haven’t noticed. It’s not a small amount — it’s enough to actually make a dent in things. They’ll probably never catch it. Do you say something?

sections.heading: Discussion questions:
sections.body:
1. Is this stealing — or just a lucky mistake that isn’t your problem to fix?

  2. Does it matter how big the company is? Does it matter how tight you are financially?

  3. What does your gut tell you — and does your gut line up with what you actually believe about integrity?

  4. If someone from this group found out you kept it, what would you say to explain yourself? Does that answer satisfy you?

Luke 16:10 “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.”

Proverbs 11:1 “A false balance is an abomination to the Lord, but a just weight is his delight.”

sections.heading: SCENARIO 4 · RELATIONSHIPS · THE HARD TRUTH
sections.body: Your buddy has been dating a girl for two years. You’ve watched the relationship up close and you genuinely don’t think she’s good for him — not because anything dramatic has happened, but because of a hundred small things you’ve noticed. He’s changing in ways that aren’t good. He’s starting to talk about proposing. He hasn’t asked for your opinion. Do you say something?

sections.heading: Discussion questions:
sections.body:
1. Is it your place to say anything? Does it matter that he hasn’t asked?

  2. What’s the difference between having an opinion about someone’s relationship and actually having a responsibility to speak?

  3. How do you say something like this in a way that doesn’t blow up the friendship?

  4. If you stay quiet and the marriage is hard, will you regret it? Does that change your answer?

  5. What would you want from your closest friends if the roles were reversed?

Proverbs 27:17 “Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another.”

Ephesians 4:15 “Speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ.”

sections.heading: SCENARIO 5 · FAITH UNDER PRESSURE · THE ROOM GOES QUIET
sections.body: You’re at a work dinner — clients, your boss, a few coworkers. Someone makes a joke that crosses a line — mocking Christianity directly, not subtly. Everyone laughs. They don’t know you’re a believer. You could let it go and nobody would ever know. Or you could say something. The table is already moving on. What do you do?

sections.heading: Discussion questions:
sections.body:
1. Do you say something in the moment — and if so, what do you actually say?

  2. Is staying quiet in that moment the same as being ashamed of your faith — or is it just reading the room?

  3. Does it matter that your job or a client relationship might be at stake?

  4. When’s the last time your faith actually cost you something in a social or professional setting? How did you handle it?

  5. What’s the version of this scenario that happens in your actual life — not dramatically, just quietly?

Matthew 10:32–33 “So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.”

Romans 1:16 “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.”

sections.heading: SCENARIO 6 · LOYALTY & FRIENDSHIP · THE GROUP CHAT
sections.body: Someone in your friend group — not in this Bible study — is going through a hard time and making some genuinely bad decisions. The rest of the group has started venting about him behind his back. The group chat is blowing up. Some of it is concern, some of it is just gossip dressed up as concern. You’re watching it happen in real time. What do you do?

sections.heading: Discussion questions:
sections.body:
1. Is there a difference between talking about someone out of concern and just talking about someone? How do you know which one is happening?

  2. Do you say something in the group chat — and if so, what? Or do you take it private?

  3. Does the guy who’s being talked about have any idea? Does that matter?

  4. What’s the most loving thing you can do for him right now — and for the group?

  5. Have you been the guy being talked about in a group chat before? What would you have wanted someone to do?

Proverbs 11:13 “Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered.”

Matthew 18:15 “If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone.”

sections.heading: HOW TO CLOSE
sections.body:
After the last scenario, don’t just end — land it with one final question to the whole group:

“Of everything we talked about tonight — which scenario hit closest to your actual life right now?”

Let every guy answer. Then close in prayer — pray specifically over the real situations that surfaced in the room. This session works best when the scenarios stop being hypothetical and start connecting to something guys are actually living.

Leader tip: The best case study sessions are the ones where someone eventually says ‘okay this actually happened to me.’ When that moment comes, stop the format entirely and let the group respond to the real thing. That’s worth more than finishing the scenarios.

title: What Would Your Life Look Like If You Trusted God Completely?

sections.heading: HOW THIS SESSION WORKS
sections.body:
This is a Socratic session — meaning there is no prepared teaching or lecture. Your job as leader is not to have the answers. Your job is to ask the question, keep the conversation honest, and drop in the anchor verses when the group needs grounding. Let the men in the room do the work.

The session has one central question. Everything else — the follow-up questions, the anchor verses, the pushback prompts — exists to serve that one question. If the conversation goes somewhere unexpected and real, follow it.

“What would your life actually look like if you trusted God completely — and why don’t you?”

sections.heading: OPEN WITH THIS — NO SETUP NEEDED
sections.body: The second half of this question — ‘why don’t you’ — is where it gets real. Don’t let guys answer the first part and skip the second. Hold them to both.

sections.heading: ANCHOR VERSES — DROP IN AS NEEDED
sections.body:
Proverbs 3:5–6 “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.”

Matthew 6:25–27 “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life… Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?”

Philippians 4:6–7 “Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer… the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts.”

Psalm 23:1 “The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.”

Romans 8:28 “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.”

sections.heading: FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS — USE IF CONVERSATION STALLS
sections.body:
1. What area of your life do you trust God with the least right now? Why that one?

  2. Is there a difference between saying you trust God and actually living like you do? Where does that gap show up in your life?

  3. What are you most afraid would happen if you let go of control in a specific area and actually trusted God with it?

  4. Has there ever been a time you trusted God with something hard and it actually worked out — or didn’t? How did that shape how much you trust Him now?

  5. Do you think trusting God means being passive — just waiting — or does it include action? Where’s the line?

  6. Romans 8:28 says all things work together for good. Do you actually believe that right now, in your real life? Or does it feel more like a bumper sticker?

  7. What would you do differently this week if you genuinely believed God had your life handled?

  8. Is control something you hold onto because you don’t trust God — or because you don’t trust yourself to handle it if things go wrong?

sections.heading: PUSHBACK PROMPTS — USE TO DEEPEN, NOT TO WIN
sections.body:
1. That sounds like trust — but what would it actually cost you to live that way? What would have to change? — use when someone describes trust without naming what it would require of them

  2. Is that actually faith, or is it just acceptance that you can’t control everything anyway? — use to distinguish real trust from passive resignation

  3. Where in your life are you still holding the wheel with both hands? — use when someone says they trust God generally but hasn’t named anything specific

sections.heading: HOW TO CLOSE
sections.body:
This question tends to surface real anxiety, real control issues, and sometimes real grief over prayers that weren’t answered the way guys hoped. Close carefully and specifically:

“What’s one thing you’re going to actually trust God with this week — not in theory, but for real?”

Let each guy name something specific out loud. Then close in prayer over each one by name — this is one of the most powerful ways to end a session like this.

title: What’s the Difference Between a Good Man and a Godly Man?

sections.heading: HOW THIS SESSION WORKS
sections.body:
This is a Socratic session — meaning there is no prepared teaching or lecture. Your job as leader is not to have the answers. Your job is to ask the question, keep the conversation honest, and drop in the anchor verses when the group needs grounding. Let the men in the room do the work.

The session has one central question. Everything else — the follow-up questions, the anchor verses, the pushback prompts — exists to serve that one question. If the conversation goes somewhere unexpected and real, follow it.

“What’s the actual difference between a good man and a godly man — and which one are you trying to be?”

sections.heading: OPEN WITH THIS — NO SETUP NEEDED
sections.body: Most guys have never been asked to separate these two. The assumption is they’re the same thing. Start there — ‘Are they the same?’ — and let the group figure it out themselves.

sections.heading: ANCHOR VERSES — DROP IN AS NEEDED
sections.body:
Romans 5:7–8 “For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die — but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

Isaiah 64:6 “All our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.”

Matthew 19:17 “And he said to him, ‘Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good.’”

Galatians 2:20 “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.”

Titus 2:11–12 “For the grace of God has appeared… training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives.”

sections.heading: FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS — USE IF CONVERSATION STALLS
sections.body:
1. Can you be a genuinely good man without God? Most people around you would say yes — do you agree?

  2. Is morality enough? Can a man be honest, generous, and kind — and still be missing something fundamental?

  3. What’s the motivation difference? A good man does right things — what does a godly man do differently, and why?

  4. Paul says it’s no longer he who lives but Christ. What does that actually look like practically — or does it just sound good?

  5. If goodness can exist without God, why does God bother? What does faith actually add to the equation?

  6. Be honest — are you mostly trying to be a good man by the world’s standard, or are you genuinely after something different?

  7. Is godliness attractive to you — or does it feel like a ceiling on what you could be?

sections.heading: PUSHBACK PROMPTS — USE TO DEEPEN, NOT TO WIN
sections.body:
1. You said a good man and a godly man are basically the same — then what’s the cross for? — use when someone collapses the distinction too quickly

  2. Is that actually what you want — or what you think you’re supposed to want? — use when someone gives a spiritually correct answer that feels disconnected from how they actually live

  3. Name a godly man you’ve personally known. What made him different from just a good guy? — use to move from abstract to concrete

sections.heading: HOW TO CLOSE
sections.body:
This one tends to end with guys realizing they’ve been aiming at goodness rather than godliness — which is a meaningful distinction. Close with:

“If goodness is the floor and godliness is the ceiling — which one have you actually been reaching for?”

Let it sit. Close in prayer — that the group would stop settling for good when God is offering something better.

title: Is It Possible to Follow Jesus and Still Be Ambitious?

sections.heading: HOW THIS SESSION WORKS
sections.body:
This is a Socratic session — meaning there is no prepared teaching or lecture. Your job as leader is not to have the answers. Your job is to ask the question, keep the conversation honest, and drop in the anchor verses when the group needs grounding. Let the men in the room do the work.

The session has one central question. Everything else — the follow-up questions, the anchor verses, the pushback prompts — exists to serve that one question. If the conversation goes somewhere unexpected and real, follow it.

“Is it possible to follow Jesus and still be ambitious — or does one eventually have to lose to the other?”

sections.heading: OPEN WITH THIS — NO SETUP NEEDED
sections.body: This one tends to split the room fast. Some guys will say yes immediately, others will push back. Don’t resolve the tension early — that tension is the whole point. Let it run.

sections.heading: ANCHOR VERSES — DROP IN AS NEEDED
sections.body:
Colossians 3:23 “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.”

Matthew 6:33 “But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

Proverbs 16:3 “Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established.”

Mark 10:43–44 “Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.”

1 Timothy 6:6 “Godliness with contentment is great gain.”

sections.heading: FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS — USE IF CONVERSATION STALLS
sections.body:
1. What’s the difference between ambition that serves God and ambition that competes with Him? How do you know which one you have?

  2. Is there a version of ambition that’s actually God-honoring? What does that look like versus what you see rewarded around you?

  3. Jesus says the greatest among you will be the servant of all. Can someone be both servant-hearted and deeply ambitious at the same time?

  4. Do you think God cares whether you succeed professionally? Does He have an opinion about your career?

  5. Is your ambition pointed at building something for God, building something for yourself, or do you not know the difference yet?

  6. Have you ever felt like your drive to succeed was pulling you away from your faith — not dramatically, just slowly? What did that look like?

  7. What would ‘seeking first the kingdom’ actually change about how you approach your work this week? Be specific.

  8. Is there a number — a salary, a title, a goal — you’ve told yourself will finally make you okay? What happens after you hit it?

sections.heading: PUSHBACK PROMPTS — USE TO DEEPEN, NOT TO WIN
sections.body:
1. So where does your ambition actually come from — conviction or comparison? — use when someone says their ambition is God-driven but can’t explain how

  2. Is that actually what you believe — or what you’ve been told you should believe? — use when an answer sounds more theological than personal

  3. What would you do differently tomorrow if you believed that answer completely? — use to move from theory to practice

sections.heading: HOW TO CLOSE
sections.body:
This one often ends without a clean resolution — and that’s okay. Close with:

“Where is your ambition actually taking you — and is that where you want to go?”

Let each guy sit with it. No need to answer out loud. Close in prayer over the specific ambitions in the room — that they’d be surrendered to God’s purposes, not just personal ones.

title: What Does It Actually Mean to Be a Man of God?

sections.heading: Intro
sections.body: Format: Socratic discussion · No prepared teaching · ~45–60 min

sections.heading: HOW THIS SESSION WORKS
sections.body:
This is a Socratic session — meaning there is no prepared teaching or lecture. Your job as leader is not to have the answers. Your job is to ask the question, keep the conversation honest, and drop in the anchor verses when the group needs grounding. Let the men in the room do the work.

The session has one central question. Everything else — the follow-up questions, the anchor verses, the pushback prompts — exists to serve that one question. If the conversation goes somewhere unexpected and real, follow it.

“What does it actually mean to be a man of God — and are you one?”

sections.heading: OPEN WITH THIS — NO SETUP NEEDED
sections.body: Don’t explain it. Don’t soften it. Just ask it and let the room sit with it for ten full seconds before anyone speaks. The silence is part of the question.

sections.heading: ANCHOR VERSES — DROP IN AS NEEDED
sections.body:
Don’t read these upfront. Hold them and bring them in when the conversation needs grounding or a new angle.

Micah 6:8 “He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?”

1 Timothy 4:8 “For while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.”

1 Corinthians 16:13 “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong.”

Proverbs 20:7 “The righteous man walks in his integrity; blessed are his children after him.”

sections.heading: FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS — USE IF CONVERSATION STALLS
sections.body:
Pick whatever fits. You don’t need all of them — one good follow-up can open an hour of conversation.

  1. Is ‘man of God’ something you become, or something you already are the moment you follow Jesus? Does that distinction matter?

  2. What’s the difference between a good man and a godly man? Can you be one without the other?

  3. If someone followed you around for a week with no warning — your work, your phone, your private life — would they conclude you’re a man of God?

  4. The culture has a picture of what a strong man looks like. Scripture has a different one. Where do they conflict most for you personally?

  5. Is godliness something you pursue or something that happens to you as a byproduct of following Jesus? What’s the difference in practice?

  6. Are you actively becoming the man you want to be — or are you mostly just hoping you’ll get there eventually?

  7. Micah 6:8 boils it down to three things: justice, kindness, humility. Which of the three is hardest for you right now?

sections.heading: PUSHBACK PROMPTS — USE TO DEEPEN, NOT TO WIN
sections.body:
If an answer feels too easy or too safe, push back gently. These aren’t gotcha questions — they’re invitations to go deeper.

  1. That’s a good answer — but is that actually true of your life right now, or is it what you think it should look like? — use when an answer sounds right but feels rehearsed

  2. Would the people closest to you agree with that? What would they say? — use when someone describes themselves more generously than they might deserve

  3. What would have to change in your actual daily life for that to be true? — use when someone gives a theoretical answer

sections.heading: HOW TO CLOSE
sections.body:
Don’t summarize or teach at the end. Instead, close with one final question that each guy sits with personally:

“Based on this conversation — what’s one thing you know needs to change?”

Let each guy answer briefly. Then close in prayer — pray over what was actually said in the room, not a generic prayer.

sections.heading: WHY THIS PASSAGE
sections.body:
Six weeks in, the group has covered a lot of ground — the call, purpose, character, ambition, and relationships. All of that assumes one thing: that there’s an actual ongoing connection between you and God. This week you look directly at that connection.

Prayer is one of those topics where most guys will privately admit they struggle. It can feel awkward, one-sided, or like something you only do when things get bad. But Jesus doesn’t treat prayer as a crisis tool or a religious ritual — He treats it like a conversation with someone who already knows you and is already listening. That changes how the whole thing feels.

This week isn’t about guilt over not praying enough. It’s about getting honest about what’s actually going on between each guy and God — and what it could look like to make that more real.

“Prayer isn’t you convincing God to care. It’s you admitting that you already need Him.”

sections.heading: SCRIPTURE PASSAGES (ESV)
sections.body:
Matthew 6:5–13 — The Lord’s Prayer

5 And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward.

6 But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.

7 And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words.

8 Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

9 Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.

10 Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.

11 Give us this day our daily bread,

12 and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

13 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.

Philippians 4:6–7

6 Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.

7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Romans 8:26

26 Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE to open. These are designed to get guys being honest about where they actually are with prayer before diving into the passages.

  1. On a scale of 1–10, how would you honestly rate your prayer life right now? What’s driving that number? — disarming because everyone can answer it and it’s rarely a 10

  2. When do you actually pray? Like really — what does it look like, when does it happen, and what do you say? — practical and honest, cuts past the theoretical fast

  3. Has there ever been a time when you prayed and something actually happened? What was that like? — positive angle — good if you want to open with faith before getting to the struggle

  4. What makes prayer feel awkward or hard for you? Be honest — most guys feel this way. — normalizes the struggle right away, levels the room

Leader tip: This topic can bring out shame quickly — guys who feel like they should be praying more and aren’t. Set the tone early that this isn’t a guilt session. You’re all figuring it out.

sections.heading: 2 — CONTEXT (5–8 MIN)
sections.body:
After reading through the passages together, share this background before jumping into discussion:

Matthew 6:5–13 — How Jesus Taught Us to Pray

  • Jesus gives this teaching right in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount — it’s not a side topic, it’s central.

  • He starts with what NOT to do: don’t perform for people, don’t use prayer to look spiritual.

  • Then He gives the model — not a script to repeat, but a structure: worship, surrender, daily needs, forgiveness, protection.

  • The tone is relational. “Our Father” — not ‘Almighty Creator.’ Jesus is telling us how God wants to be approached.

  • Key line: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” So prayer isn’t about informing God. It’s about relationship.

Philippians 4:6–7 — Pray Instead of Worry

  • Paul writes this from prison — not from a comfortable life where anxiety is easy to manage.

  • The command isn’t ‘don’t feel anxious.’ It’s ‘when you’re anxious, pray instead of just spiraling.’

  • The result isn’t that the problem disappears — it’s that a peace that doesn’t make logical sense shows up anyway.

  • Notice ‘with thanksgiving’ — gratitude is built into the prayer, even before the answer comes.

Romans 8:26 — You Don’t Have to Have It Together

  • Paul acknowledges straight up: we don’t always know what to pray for. That’s normal, not a failure.

  • The Spirit steps in when we don’t have the words — which means showing up matters even when you feel stuck.

  • This verse is permission to pray imperfectly. God isn’t waiting for your eloquence. He’s waiting for you.

“God doesn’t need your perfect words. He needs your actual presence.”

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: YOUR ACTUAL PRAYER LIFE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
These questions get honest about where guys really are with prayer — not where they think they should be. Pick the ones that fit the room.

  1. Do you actually have a prayer life, or is most of your praying reactive — when something goes wrong or you need something?

  2. What does prayer feel like for you most of the time — connected, dry, obligatory, natural, something else?

  3. Jesus says God already knows what you need before you ask. If that’s true, why do you think prayer still matters? Does that change how you think about it?

  4. Is there something you’ve been anxious about that you’ve been carrying on your own instead of bringing to God? What’s kept you from praying about it?

  5. Romans 8:26 says the Spirit helps us when we don’t know what to pray. Have you ever experienced that — a moment where you just didn’t have words but felt something anyway?

  6. Do you pray differently in public vs. in private? What does that gap tell you?

  7. Have you ever prayed for something and felt like God didn’t answer? How did that affect your prayer life after?

  8. What’s the biggest thing keeping you from praying more consistently — honestly? Time, doubt, feeling unworthy, not knowing how, something else?

Leader tip: Question 7 is a big one — unanswered prayer is something almost every guy in the room has experienced and few talk about. If it comes up, don’t rush to give a theological answer. Just let guys process it first.

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: WHAT PRAYER COULD ACTUALLY LOOK LIKE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Move from diagnosis to direction. These questions help guys think practically about what a real prayer life could look like for them — not a religious ideal, but something they’d actually do.

  1. Jesus’ model prayer covers worship, surrender, daily needs, forgiveness, and protection. Which of those do you never pray? Which one do you need most right now?

  2. What would it look like for you to build even 5 minutes of prayer into your day? What would have to change practically?

  3. Philippians 4:6 says pray ‘with thanksgiving.’ What’s something specific you could be more genuinely thankful for right now — even in the middle of a hard season?

  4. Is there a situation in your life right now where you’ve been trying to figure it out yourself instead of actually asking God? What would it look like to surrender that?

  5. Do you pray with other people — out loud, with friends or family? If not, what makes that feel weird? If so, what’s made it feel natural?

  6. What would it look like to pray specifically and boldly — asking God for something real and concrete — instead of vaguely? Is there something you’ve been afraid to ask for?

  7. What do you think would actually change in your life if prayer became a real daily habit rather than something occasional?

  8. If you treated prayer like a conversation with someone who loves you and is actually listening — instead of a religious task — what would you say to God right now?

Leader tip: Question 8 is a good one to end this section with and let sit for a moment before closing. It often opens something up in guys that the rest of the discussion was building toward.

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Jesus didn’t give the disciples a theology lecture on prayer. He showed them how to do it and then said ‘pray like this.’ It’s meant to be practiced, not perfected. The goal isn’t a flawless prayer life — it’s an honest one. Showing up. Bringing what’s actually going on. Trusting that He’s listening.

“The most spiritual thing you can do today might just be to stop and actually talk to God about what’s really going on.”

Leave the group with one of these to carry into the week:

  1. Pick one thing you’ve been carrying on your own this week and commit to actually praying about it every day until the next meeting. Tell the group what it is. — accountability built in before they leave

  2. Try praying out loud for 5 minutes this week — even if it feels weird. Just talk to God like you’d talk to someone you trust. Report back next week on what it was like.

  3. Use the Lord’s Prayer as a framework once this week — go through each section and make it personal and specific to your actual life right now.

Close by actually praying together as a group. Let it be real — not polished. If guys feel comfortable, let more than one person pray. Model what the whole session was about.

Leader tip: This is a great week to do something different for the close: instead of one person praying, go around and let each guy say one sentence out loud to God — even just one thing they’re thankful for or need. It’s low pressure and it puts prayer into practice right there in the room.

title: How You Love People Is How You Love God

sections.heading: WHY THIS PASSAGE
sections.body:
Five weeks in, the group has covered the call, purpose, character, and what drives you underneath the surface. This week turns it outward: does any of that actually show up in how you treat people?

It’s easy to think of faith as a private, internal thing — between you and God. But Jesus collapses that in two sentences. Love God, love people. He says everything hangs on those two commands. James says faith that doesn’t produce action is dead. John goes even further: you can’t claim to love a God you can’t see if you can’t love the person standing right in front of you.

For guys in their mid-20s, this hits in specific places — how you treat your girlfriend or wife, how you talk to your parents, how you handle conflict with friends, how you treat people at work who can do nothing for you. That’s where this gets real.

“The way you treat people is a direct reflection of what’s actually going on between you and God.”

sections.heading: SCRIPTURE PASSAGES (ESV)
sections.body:
Matthew 22:36–40

36 “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?”

37 And he said to him, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.

38 This is the great and first commandment.

39 And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

40 On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.”

James 2:14–17

14 What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?

15 If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food,

16 and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?

17 So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

1 John 4:20

20 If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE to open. These are designed to get guys thinking about real relationships before the passage, not abstract concepts.

  1. Who in your life is genuinely hard for you to love right now? You don’t have to name them — just be honest that they exist. — vulnerable opener that levels the room fast

  2. Think of someone who’s had a real impact on your life — not because of what they said, but because of how they treated you. What did they do? — positive angle that gets guys thinking about love in action

  3. On a scale of 1–10, how well do you think the people closest to you feel loved by you? What do you think they’d actually say? — self-awareness question, slightly convicting but not heavy

  4. Is there a relationship in your life right now that you’ve been avoiding or letting drift? What’s behind that? — good if the group is comfortable enough for honesty

Leader tip: This topic is personal in a different way than the last few weeks — it touches specific people in guys’ lives. Keep it safe early. Let guys go as deep as they want, but don’t push.

sections.heading: 2 — CONTEXT (5–8 MIN)
sections.body:
After reading through the passages together, share this background before jumping into discussion:

Matthew 22:36–40 — The Two Greatest Commandments

  • A religious expert asks Jesus which commandment is the greatest — trying to trap him.

  • Jesus doesn’t pick one. He gives two, and says the second is ‘like’ the first — they’re inseparable.

  • “All the Law and the Prophets hang on these.” Every other command flows from these two.

  • You can’t fully obey the first without the second. Loving God and loving people are two sides of the same coin.

James 2:14–17 — Faith Without Works

  • James is writing to believers who say the right things but aren’t living them out.

  • His point isn’t that works earn salvation — it’s that real faith always produces action.

  • Saying “I’ll pray for you” and walking away when someone has a real need is the example he uses.

  • Dead faith talks. Living faith moves.

1 John 4:20 — You Can’t Have One Without the Other

  • John is as direct as it gets: if you say you love God but treat people badly, you’re lying.

  • His logic: if you can’t love the person right in front of you, you don’t actually love God.

  • This isn’t about being perfect — it’s about the direction of your life and what your relationships reveal about your heart.

“Your relationships aren’t separate from your faith. They are the evidence of it.”

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: HOW YOU ACTUALLY TREAT PEOPLE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
These questions get specific. The goal isn’t guilt — it’s honest self-examination. Pick the ones that fit the room.

  1. If the people closest to you — family, friends, coworkers — described how you treat them, what do you think they’d say?

  2. Is there a gap between how you act around this group or at church versus how you treat people at home or at work? What causes that?

  3. John says if you can’t love your brother, you can’t love God. Is there anyone in your life that verse is pointed directly at right now?

  4. How do you treat people who can do nothing for you — service workers, people you pass by, people lower on the social ladder? Be honest.

  5. Is there someone in your life you’ve written off, given up on, or decided isn’t worth the effort? What happened there?

  6. Do the people closest to you feel prioritized by you — or do they mostly get what’s left after everything else?

  7. How do you handle conflict with people you care about? Do you lean in or pull away? What does that pattern cost you?

  8. Is there an apology you’ve been putting off? A conversation you’ve been avoiding? What’s actually keeping you from it?

Leader tip: Question 8 often lands the hardest — most guys have something specific come to mind immediately. Don’t rush past it. If someone names something real, let the group sit with it before moving on.

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: LOVE IN ACTION (10 MIN)
sections.body:
James says faith without works is dead. These questions look at what active, practical love actually looks like — not as a feeling, but as a choice.

  1. James uses a practical example — someone needs food and clothes and you just say ‘be warm and filled.’ Where in your life are you doing the spiritual version of that?

  2. What’s the difference between loving someone and liking them? Can you love someone you don’t particularly like? What does that look like?

  3. Jesus says love your neighbor as yourself. How well do you actually know your neighbors — literally or figuratively? What would it look like to change that?

  4. Who in your life needs something from you right now that you’ve been meaning to give but haven’t? Time, a conversation, help, forgiveness?

  5. Is there a relationship in your life where you’ve been waiting for the other person to make the first move? What would it look like for you to go first?

  6. How do you love people when they don’t deserve it or haven’t earned it? What does that actually require of you?

  7. What would the guys in this room say is the most loving thing someone has ever done for them? What made it land?

  8. If you took Matthew 22:39 seriously this week — love your neighbor as yourself — what would be the first thing you’d change?

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Jesus didn’t say the greatest commandment is to have the right theology, go to church, or read your Bible. He said love God, love people — and everything else hangs on those two things. That’s not permission to skip the other stuff. It’s a reminder that all of it is supposed to produce this: a man who actually loves the people in his life well.

“The proof of your faith isn’t what you believe. It’s how you treat people when it costs you something.”

Leave the group with one of these to carry into the week — something specific and doable:

  1. Name one person you’re going to reach out to this week that you’ve been putting off. What are you going to do? — gets guys to commit to something concrete before they leave

  2. Is there a relationship you need to repair? What’s one step you could take toward that this week — not the whole conversation, just one step?

  3. Who in your life needs to feel loved by you right now and doesn’t? What would it look like to actually do something about that this week?

Close in prayer — pray over specific relationships in the room. If guys named people or situations during discussion, bring those into the prayer. It makes the whole thing feel real and connected.

Leader tip: Consider ending with a challenge: each guy texts or calls one person before the next meeting just to check in — no agenda, just love in action. Report back next week on what happened.

sections.heading: WHY THIS PASSAGE
sections.body:
Three weeks in, the guys have said yes to the call, they’re thinking about their purpose, and they’re working on who they are in private. Now comes the question underneath all of it: what is actually driving you? Because you can follow Jesus in theory and still be completely controlled by the pursuit of money, status, and success in practice.

This is one of the most relevant conversations you can have with a group of guys in their mid-20s. You’re all in the thick of building careers, comparing yourselves to peers, and figuring out what ‘making it’ even means. Jesus talks about money more than almost any other topic — not because money is evil, but because it competes directly with God for the throne of your life.

“You can’t serve two masters.” That’s not a suggestion. It’s a diagnosis.

sections.heading: SCRIPTURE PASSAGES (ESV)
sections.body:
Matthew 6:19–24

19 Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal,

20 but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal.

21 For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

22 The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light,

23 but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!

24 No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.

Matthew 6:33

33 But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

Luke 12:15–21

15 And he said to them, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.”

16 And he told them a parable, saying, “The land of a rich man produced plentifully,

17 and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’

18 And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods.

19 And I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.”’

20 But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’

21 So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.”

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE to open. These are designed to surface the real motivations guys carry without putting anyone on the defensive right away.

  1. What does ‘making it’ look like to you? Like if you hit it — what does that actually look like? — disarming and gets guys to name what they’re actually chasing

  2. What’s your honest relationship with money right now — stressed, chasing it, content, somewhere else? — practical and relatable for guys in their 20s

  3. Is there someone in your life — maybe someone you follow on social media — whose life you quietly want? What specifically about it? — gets at comparison and ambition without feeling churchy

  4. If your bank account and calendar showed someone else what you actually value — what would they conclude? — convicting opener if the group is ready for it

sections.heading: 2 — CONTEXT (5 MIN)
sections.body:
After reading through the passages together, share this background before jumping into discussion:

Matthew 6:19–24

  • This is from the Sermon on the Mount — Jesus’ most direct teaching on how to actually live.

  • “Treasures on earth” aren’t just bank accounts — it’s anything temporary you’re building your security on.

  • The “eye” language in v.22–23 is about where your focus goes — if your gaze is fixed on wealth, your whole life orients toward it.

  • “You cannot serve both God and money” — the word ‘serve’ means to be enslaved to. Jesus is saying one of them owns you.

Luke 12:15–21 — The Rich Fool

  • A man’s crops produce massively. His plan: build bigger barns, store everything, retire early. Sounds reasonable.

  • God calls him a fool — not because he was wealthy, but because he built his entire future on stuff that couldn’t save him.

  • The man never asked what God wanted him to do with this. He only asked what he wanted.

  • Jesus ends: “This is how it will be with whoever stores up things for themselves but is not rich toward God.”

“The question isn’t whether you have money or ambition. It’s whether money and ambition have you.”

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: WHAT YOU’RE CHASING (10 MIN)
sections.body:
These questions get at the real motivations underneath the surface. Pick the ones that fit the room — you don’t need all of them.

  1. When you imagine your life at 40, what does it look like? House, car, job, lifestyle. Where did that picture come from?

  2. Is there a number — a salary, a title, a milestone — that you’ve told yourself will finally make you feel okay? What happens when you hit it?

  3. Jesus says you’re serving one master or the other. If you’re being honest, which one is running more of your decisions right now?

  4. What do you spend most of your mental energy on during the day? Does that match what you say you value?

  5. How much does what other people have — or what they think of you — actually affect your decisions?

  6. The rich fool’s plan sounded reasonable. Are there any ‘reasonable’ plans in your life right now that don’t actually include God?

  7. Do you think there’s a version of ambition and drive that’s God-honoring? What does that look like vs. what you see around you?

  8. What would you do differently with your time or money right now if you actually believed Jesus’ promise in Matthew 6:33?

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: CONTENTMENT & ENOUGH (10 MIN)
sections.body:
The flip side of ambition is contentment — one of the hardest things to actually have in your 20s. These questions go there.

  1. Do you think contentment is something you have or something you practice? What’s the difference?

  2. Is there anything in your life right now that you have — that you once prayed for — that you’ve stopped being grateful for?

  3. What does ‘enough’ actually look like for you? Have you ever defined it, or is it always just a little more than what you have?

  4. Paul says he ‘learned’ contentment (Philippians 4:11) — it’s not natural, it’s trained. What do you think that training looks like day to day?

  5. Is social media making contentment harder for you? Be honest about how it actually affects you.

  6. What would it look like to be genuinely generous right now — at your current income, in your current situation? What’s stopping you?

  7. If the man in the parable had asked God what to do with the surplus instead of building bigger barns — what do you think God would have said?

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
The rich fool wasn’t condemned for working hard or being successful. He was condemned for leaving God completely out of the equation — for living as if the resources in his hands were his alone. The invitation in Matthew 6:33 isn’t to be poor or stop being ambitious. It’s to reorder what you’re seeking first.

“Seek first the kingdom — and all these things will be added. The promise isn’t poverty. It’s priority.”

Leave the group with one of these to carry into the week:

  1. What is one concrete way you could seek the kingdom first this week — with your time, your money, or your decisions?

  2. Is there one area where you need to loosen your grip on something you’ve been holding too tightly?

  3. What would it look like to bring God into one financial or career decision you’ve been making on your own?

Close in prayer — specifically over ambition, provision, and what it means to trust God with the outcomes.

Leader tip: Consider a 1-week challenge: each guy identifies one thing he’s been treating as a master instead of a tool — and picks one practical step to reorder it. Report back next week.

title: Who Are You When No One’s Watching?

sections.heading: WHY THIS PASSAGE
sections.body:
Week 1 you looked at the call — saying yes to following Jesus like Matthew did. Week 2 you dug into purpose and identity — the fact that you were made for something specific. Week 3 is where it gets practical: how do you actually live that out when life puts pressure on you?

Daniel is one of the most compelling figures in all of Scripture for guys in their 20s. He’s taken from everything familiar, dropped into a culture that directly opposes his values, handed every reason to compromise — and he doesn’t. Not because he’s perfect, but because he’d already decided who he was before the pressure came.

Integrity isn’t what you do when people are watching. It’s what you’ve already decided to do before the moment arrives.

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE of these to kick things off. Keep it light enough to warm up the room but pointed enough to set the theme.

  1. Have you ever done the right thing when it would have been way easier to do the wrong thing? What happened? — gets guys thinking about real moments, not theory

  2. Is there a version of you that shows up at work or around certain people that’s different from who you are here? What’s different about him? — cuts right to the theme of private vs public self

  3. What’s one area of your life where you feel like you’re constantly fighting the same battle? — honest and relatable, sets up the temptation angle

  4. Who in your life do you respect most for how they actually live — not just what they believe? What makes them different? — good if you want to start with inspiration before conviction

sections.heading: 2 — SCRIPTURE & CONTEXT (8–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Read all three passages aloud. Go around the group — keep it moving, don’t stop to comment yet.

  • Daniel 1:1–8 — Daniel resolves not to defile himself

  • Daniel 6:1–10 — Daniel prays anyway, even when it’s illegal

  • Proverbs 4:23 — Guard your heart, for everything flows from it

After reading, take 30 seconds of silence. Then give the group this context:

Context on Daniel

  • Daniel was probably 14–17 years old when he was taken to Babylon. A teenager.

  • Babylon was the most powerful empire on earth — wealthy, seductive, and totally opposed to his faith.

  • He was given a new name, new food, new education — a full-scale identity replacement.

  • In chapter 1, his decision seems small: don’t eat the king’s food. But it was a line in the sand.

  • In chapter 6, he’s now a powerful official — and he still kneels and prays, even when it could get him killed.

  • The key: Daniel didn’t decide what he stood for in the moment of pressure. He’d already decided.

Context on Proverbs 4:23

  • “Heart” in Hebrew (lev) means the center of your will, thought, and emotion — not just feelings.

  • To “guard” it means to be intentional about what you let in and what you dwell on.

  • Everything you do flows from what’s happening internally — your habits, your choices, your character.

“Who you are in private is who you actually are. Everything else is performance.”

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: THE PRIVATE LIFE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Daniel’s integrity wasn’t built in the lion’s den — it was built in the small daily decisions that came before it. These questions go there.

  1. Is who you are in private consistent with who you are around other people? Where’s the biggest gap?

  2. What do your habits look like when no one’s holding you accountable — what you watch, how you spend your time, what you think about?

  3. Proverbs says everything flows from the heart. What are you currently letting into your heart that you know isn’t helping you?

  4. Is there a line in the sand — something you’ve decided you won’t do — or are most of your decisions made in the moment?

  5. When you’re under pressure — stressed, tired, alone — who do you become? Is that who you want to be?

  6. What would change if you lived every day like God actually sees everything? Not out of fear — but out of that being real to you?

  7. Is there something you’re doing privately right now that you’d be ashamed for the guys in this room to know about? — hard question — only use if the group is ready for it

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: PRESSURE & COMPROMISE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Daniel faced real, external pressure to compromise — not just internal temptation. These questions look at the moments where integrity actually gets tested.

  1. What’s the biggest source of pressure in your life right now to be someone you’re not?

  2. Have you ever compromised on something you said you believed in because the cost felt too high? What happened?

  3. Daniel made his decision before the pressure hit — he ‘resolved’ in chapter 1. Do you have any convictions like that? Things you’ve pre-decided?

  4. Where in your life do you feel the most tempted to just go along with everyone else to avoid the friction?

  5. Is there a situation in your life right now where you know what the right thing is but you haven’t done it yet? What’s holding you back?

  6. What would it look like to be the Daniel in your friend group, your workplace, your family? What would have to change?

  7. Do you think it’s possible to maintain integrity in your 20s without a community around you holding you to it? Why or why not?

  8. What’s one area where you’ve been slowly drifting from who you want to be? When did it start?

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Daniel didn’t end up in the lion’s den because he was reckless. He ended up there because he was consistent. His integrity in the small things built the character that held in the big moment. That’s how it works for all of us — character is built slowly, in private, long before anyone’s watching.

“You don’t rise to the level of your intentions. You fall to the level of your habits.”

Leave the group with one of these to sit with this week:

  1. What is one private habit or pattern you need to change this week — not for anyone else, but because of who you actually want to become?

  2. Is there one area where you need to ‘resolve’ — pre-decide — before the moment of pressure comes?

  3. What would the guy you want to be in 10 years tell the version of you right now to start doing differently?

Close in prayer. If the conversation got personal, pray specifically over what came up — that makes it real and keeps the group connected beyond the meeting.

Leader tip: Consider ending with a 1-week challenge: each guy picks one thing they’re going to do differently in private this week and shares it with the group. Check in on it next week. Accountability is where this theme gets legs.

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE of these to open — you don’t need all of them. Just get guys talking.

  1. If you could wake up tomorrow doing anything with your life — and money wasn’t a factor — what would it be? Why don’t you think that’s realistic?

  2. What did you think you’d be doing with your life at 10 years old? How’s that working out? —

  3. Is there something you feel like you were made to do but haven’t done yet? What’s stopping you?

  4. When someone asks what you do, do you actually feel like that’s who you are? Or does it feel off?

sections.heading: 2 — SCRIPTURE & CONTEXT (8–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Go around and read both passages aloud. Keep it moving — don’t comment yet, just read.

  • Jeremiah 1:4–10

  • Ephesians 2:10

After reading, give 30–60 seconds of silence. Then share this context before jumping into discussion:

Context on Jeremiah

  • He was young — likely a teenager or early 20s when God called him.

  • He was from a small town. Nobody. Not a religious celebrity.

  • His immediate response: “I don’t know how to speak. I’m too young.”

  • God’s response: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before you were born, I set you apart.”

  • Jeremiah didn’t feel ready. God said he already was.

Context on Ephesians 2:10

  • “Poiema” — the Greek word translated “workmanship” — is where we get the word “poem.”

  • You are not an accident. You are something God crafted with intention.

  • The “good works” were prepared in advance — meaning purpose isn’t something you create. It’s something you walk into.

“God’s calling on your life isn’t based on how ready you feel — it’s based on who He says you are.”

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: THE EXCUSES (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Jeremiah’s first move when God called him was to explain why he couldn’t do it. Most of us do the same thing. Use any of these — you don’t need all of them. Follow the energy in the room.

  1. What’s your version of “I’m too young / I don’t know how”? What do you tell yourself disqualifies you?

  2. Is there something you’ve felt nudged toward — in faith, career, or relationships — that you’ve been putting off? What’s the real reason?

  3. Do you actually believe God has a specific purpose for your life — or does that feel like something that applies to other people?

  4. Have you ever talked yourself out of something before even trying? What did you tell yourself?

  5. What’s the difference between being genuinely not ready and just being scared?

  6. If a close friend described what they think you’re made for, what do you think they’d say? Does that match how you see yourself?

  7. Is there an area of your life where you’re waiting for permission to step into something — and who are you waiting for it from?

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: CREATED ON PURPOSE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Flip it from the excuses to the truth. You are God’s “poiema” — His masterpiece. That’s not a feel-good slogan; it’s a theological statement about how you were made and why. Pick the questions that fit your group.

  1. What’s one thing you’re genuinely good at that you’ve maybe never thought of as something God gave you on purpose?

  2. Are you currently living in a way that’s moving toward your purpose — or are you mostly just filling time? Be honest.

  3. What would change in your day-to-day life if you actually believed you were made for something specific?

  4. What’s the difference between your job and your calling? Do you think they have to be the same thing?

  5. If God prepared good works for you “in advance,” what do you think that means practically? Does it change how you make decisions?

  6. Is there something you keep coming back to — a problem you want to solve, a type of person you want to help, something that makes you feel alive — that you’ve been dismissing as just a feeling?

  7. Do you think God’s purpose for your life is one big thing, or a lot of small faithful things? How does that change the pressure you put on yourself?

  8. What would it look like to steward what you’re already good at more intentionally this week?

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Don’t end on a heavy question — land the plane with hope. Bring it back to Jeremiah: he was scared, unqualified, and unsure. But he went. And he became one of the most important voices in all of Scripture.

“The question isn’t whether God has a purpose for you. He does. The question is whether you’ll stop waiting to feel ready and start walking in it.”

Leave the group with one of these closing questions to sit with — they don’t have to answer out loud:

  1. What is one step — even a small one — you could take this week toward what you were made for?

  2. Is there something God has been saying to you that you’ve been ignoring? What would it look like to stop ignoring it?

  3. What would you do differently this week if you genuinely believed you were God’s workmanship, created with intention?

Close in prayer. Keep it short and specific to what actually came up in the room.
